# Product capability ledger

What this repository can sell, what exists only so that it can be measured, and what
neither has. Every verdict in the table below is derived from the code by
`tools/product-capability-ledger.mjs`; the declaration names the capability and its symbol, and
`pnpm ledger:check` fails when the two disagree in either direction.

## The four states

| state | what it means | how it is derived |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **product** | a customer can reach it | declared in a product package, no import path to the instrument, and reachable from `packages/cortex-memory/src/memory.ts` by a chain of references |
| **blocked** | implemented, tested, unreachable | declared in a product package, and **no reference reaches it from the entry** — either nothing calls it, or the only thing that calls it is itself unreachable |
| **instrument** | it exists for the measurement | declared under `tools/` or `packages/cortex-eval/` |
| **gap** | named here, absent from the code | the symbol is not declared anywhere |

A `gate` column names the configuration switch a capability sits behind, and it is checked
as a literal against the product source: a gate removed from the code and a gate that was
never there are the same defect. `D3` is **declared, not derived** — see the note below the
table.

## Why `D3` is declared and not derived

The four judgements the audit proposed were *installable* (D1), *independent* (D2),
*self-sufficient* (D3) and *callable* (D4). Three of them reduce to facts about paths and
callers, which is what the three columns above compute. D3 does not.

D3 asks whether a capability draws on state the product holds, or on arguments the caller
hands it at every call. `buildPrompt(context, question)` fails D3 by that reading, and so
does every mechanism in this repository that this ledger calls `product`, because the
product's public contract *is* `answer(question, context)`. Mechanising D3 would therefore
demote the entire product on the strength of a signature, which is a true statement about
the signature and a false one about the capability.

So the column records the claim and says what it was based on. Where the claim is doing real
work — the rows the audit grouped as "the instrument ranks, the product does not" — the
evidence is the `state` column, which is derived.

## The boundary (55 product exports)

Product exports whose only callers are the instrument. This is the audit's §3.3 argument as a
set of names rather than a paragraph, and `pnpm ledger:check` fails on a new member: a
mechanism that just became instrument-only is the change this repository wants to be told
about.

### retrieval-prototypes-in-a-product-package (5)

The natural-language-memory and embedding-memory hypotheses: a brute-force vector index, an embedding-space abstraction and rank fusion, all declared in cortex-core and reached only by cortex-eval's own prototype memory systems. They are research arms, not the shipping retrieval path (`SearchIndex` is), and a customer installs them.

`BruteForceVectorIndex`, `EmbeddingSpace`, `fuseRerank`, `norm`, `reciprocalRankFusion`

### ablation-machinery-in-a-product-package (6)

Assumption-ablation plumbing -- policy types, modality inference, plan reconciliation -- declared in cortex-core and called only by cortex-eval/src/assumption-ablation.ts. It exists so a mechanism can be turned off and measured, which is the instrument's job.

`AssembleCensus`, `AssemblePolicy`, `Resolution`, `inferTemporality`, `modalityOf`, `reconcilePlans`

### storage-adapter-reached-only-by-a-tool (1)

The concrete SQLite adapter, whose only callers are the review tool and the erasure census. The capability it serves is no longer instrument-only: `Corpus` takes any `Storage` and `assembleMemory({ storage })` is the product caller, so what remains here is this adapter and the ones beside it. They are recorded rather than moved because a backend has to live somewhere, and the package that owns it exists for exactly one reason: to be the file a deployment imports to get a file `Storage`. The distinction this group preserves is the one that matters -- the port is product, a particular engine is a leaf.

`SqliteStorage`

### provider-wiring-and-usage-accounting (22)

Provider construction (OpenAI embedding, rerankers, retry budgets, thinking modes), the profile seam that turns a deployment's environment into a provider, and token accounting. All of it lives in `cortex-ai` and none of it is reached from `memory.ts`, because `CortexMemory` takes an injected `llm` rather than building one -- so the caller is the **deployment**, and this repository ships no deployment. THE SEVEN NAMES ADDED HERE ARE A CORRECTION RATHER THAN NEW DEBT. `readApiKey`, `resolveLlmProfile`, `describeProfile`, `createLocalLLM`, `OpenAICompatibleLLM`, `ProfileError` and `PROPOSER_PROMPT_VERSION` were recorded as 'called by the product' until `isTestFile` learned the third test spelling (`packages/<pkg>/test/**`); their only in-repository callers were scripts under `packages/cortex-ai/test/profile/`, and the census had been counting those as product callers. What changed is the classification, not the code -- and the classification was wrong in the permissive direction, which is the one that lets a capability look reached when nothing in the product reaches it. THE RECIPE IS INSTEAD VERIFIED WHERE IT IS WRITTEN: `docs/USER-MANUAL.md` documents this exact construction (`new OpenAICompatibleLLM({ ...resolveLlmProfile({ backend: 'remote' }, process.env) })`) in a fenced example, and `tools/manual-examples.mjs` compiles all 35 examples against the packages' built declarations on every push -- so a renamed export or a changed profile shape fails the build at the manual's own line number. The unit surface behind it is four test files (`profile.test.ts`, `local-llm.test.ts`, `llm.test.ts`, `profile-transport.test.ts`), and the two files these exports are declared in -- `profile.ts` and `local/llm.ts` -- read 100% on all four coverage measures, which is a per-file gate rather than a summary. The audit's §3.4 row 10 still stands as the open question: env-to-option mapping sits in `bench/`, so a customer configuring a provider writes code where the harness writes a variable -- and the resolution is the documented recipe, not a second implementation.

`DEFAULT_RETRY_BUDGET_MS`, `DEFAULT_RETRY_TIMEOUT_MS`, `LLMReranker`, `OpenAICompatibleLLM`, `OpenAICompatibleReranker`, `OpenAIEmbedding`, `PROPOSER_PROMPT_VERSION`, `ProfileError`, `ProviderContentRefusal`, `ThinkingMode`, `UsageSnapshot`, `UsageTally`, `createLocalLLM`, `createUsageTally`, `describeProfile`, `llmUsage`, `makeRerankPipelineFactory`, `observeUsage`, `readApiKey`, `resetRetryStats`, `resolveLlmProfile`, `usageDelta`

### census-and-probe-tooling (14)

The caller census's own public surface and the knowledge probe's helpers: measurement instruments written in a product package because that is where their types were easiest to reach. They are the reason this gate exists, so they are recorded as the first debt rather than the last. This group grows whenever a tool imports another helper from `cortex-core` -- the capability ledger's own three imports (`isBarrelFile`, `stripComments`, `stripStringContent`) landed here on their first run, which is the gate correctly reporting on itself.

`buildCensusReport`, `censusPackage`, `edgeId`, `expandTyped`, `extractedSpan`, `fillBudget`, `isBarrelFile`, `kindsIn`, `listOrphans`, `listReferencedLocally`, `listUnreferenced`, `renderBlock`, `stripComments`, `stripStringContent`

### reply-and-decline-census-helpers (4)

Helpers of the failure censuses: how a reply is classified, what a declined item is, what a question asks for. Each is the product's own vocabulary read back by a tool, which is the cheapest possible kind of breach and the one that is easiest to leave: the product's behaviour is not affected, but the tool is the only consumer of the classifier.

`DECLINE_TOKEN`, `asksForCount`, `classifyReply`, `declinedItems`

### competitor-bridge (2)

The adapter that presents the product as a `MemorySystem` for a competitor's harness, and the distillation hook the review page reads. Instrument by design; recorded so that 'instrument-only' is a decision on the record rather than an accident of where the file was created.

`CortexSessionProvider`, `distillationOf`

### the-competitor-table-s-own-adapter (1)

`CortexProductProvider` is the shipped arm in the shape a retrieval harness asks for, and its only caller is `tools/competitor-product.mjs` -- which is the property that makes it worth having. A comparison whose cortex row is a bare session adapter measures a configuration nobody installs, so the product needs one seam that a harness knowing nothing about its internals can drive. It is not a capability a deployment calls; it is the instrument's handle on the product, declared in the product because the reverse dependency (`cortex-eval` importing `cortex-memory`) is the allowed direction.

`CortexProductProvider`
